roadmaps.title: C Programming
roadmaps.description: Master procedural programming, memory layout, pointers, structures, and low-level system interaction.

topics.title: Basics & Syntax
topics.explanation: C is a general-purpose, procedural computer programming language supporting structured programming, lexical variable scope, and recursion, with a static type system.

practiceQuestions.q: What is the difference between static and global variables?
practiceQuestions.a: Global variables have file scope and external linkage by default, whereas static variables declared outside functions have internal linkage (confined to that translation unit).

practiceQuestions.q: What happens when integer overflow occurs in signed vs unsigned integers?
practiceQuestions.a: Signed integer overflow is undefined behavior in C. Unsigned integer overflow wraps around using modulo arithmetic (2^n).

topics.title: Pointers & Dynamic Memory
topics.explanation: Pointers store memory addresses of variables. Dynamic memory allocation allocates memory on the heap at runtime.

practiceQuestions.q: What is a dangling pointer and how to avoid it?
practiceQuestions.a: A dangling pointer points to memory that has already been deallocated. Avoid by setting ptr = NULL immediately after free(ptr).

practiceQuestions.q: Explain function pointers with a real use case.
practiceQuestions.a: Function pointers store addresses of functions, enabling callbacks, event handling, and custom comparator functions like in qsort().

topics.title: Structures, Unions & File I/O
topics.explanation: Structures group different data types under one name. Memory alignment pads structs for efficient CPU word-boundary access.

practiceQuestions.q: What is structure padding in C?
practiceQuestions.a: Compilers insert empty padding bytes between struct members to align them to natural CPU memory word boundaries (e.g. 4 or 8 bytes).

roadmaps.title: C++
roadmaps.description: Object-oriented programming, STL containers, iterators, templates, and modern C++17/20.

topics.title: Classes, Objects & Virtual Functions
topics.explanation: C++ brings object-oriented paradigms with RAII, virtual tables for runtime polymorphism, and encapsulation.

practiceQuestions.q: How does vtable and vptr work in C++ dynamic polymorphism?
practiceQuestions.a: Each class with virtual functions gets a static vtable (array of function pointers). Each object gets a hidden pointer (_vptr) pointing to its class vtable.

topics.title: Standard Template Library (STL)
topics.explanation: STL provides powerful template-based data structures and algorithms optimized for peak performance in competitive programming.

practiceQuestions.q: Difference between std::map and std::unordered_map?
practiceQuestions.a: std::map uses a Red-Black Tree with O(log N) operations and sorted keys. std::unordered_map uses a hash table with O(1) average lookup and unordered keys.

topics.title: Modern C++ (C++11 to C++20)
topics.explanation: Modern C++ eliminates raw pointer ownership bugs using RAII smart pointers and achieves zero-cost transfers with move semantics.
topics.codeExample:
auto ptr = std::make_unique<int>(42);
auto lambda = [](int x, int y) { return x + y; };

practiceQuestions.q: Difference between unique_ptr and shared_ptr?
practiceQuestions.a: std::unique_ptr has exclusive ownership with zero overhead over raw pointers. std::shared_ptr uses reference counting on a control block for shared ownership.

roadmaps.title: Java
roadmaps.description: JVM architecture, Garbage Collection, Multithreading, Collections Framework, and Java 8 Streams.

topics.title: JVM Architecture & Memory Areas
topics.explanation: Java code compiles to bytecode which runs on any Java Virtual Machine. Memory is divided into Heap, Stack, Metaspace, PC Registers, and Native Method Stack.

practiceQuestions.q: Why is Java platform independent but JVM platform dependent?
practiceQuestions.a: Java compiles to standardized platform-neutral bytecode (.class). However, the JVM translating this bytecode into native machine instructions must be built specifically for each host OS.

topics.title: Collections Framework & Streams
topics.explanation: Collections framework offers data structure implementations. In Java 8+, HashMap converts collision buckets into Red-Black Trees when bucket size exceeds TREEIFY_THRESHOLD (8).
topics.codeExample:
List<String> names = Arrays.asList("Alex", "Bob", "Alice");
names.stream().filter(n -> n.startsWith("A")).forEach(System.out::println);

practiceQuestions.q: Explain internal working of HashMap in Java 8.
practiceQuestions.a: Uses an array of Node buckets indexed by (n-1) & hash(key). If collisions exceed 8 nodes and capacity is >= 64, linked lists convert into balanced trees for O(log N) worst-case retrieval.

topics.title: Multithreading & Concurrency
topics.explanation: Java provides built-in multithreading. Synchronized ensures mutual exclusion on object monitors, while volatile prevents thread-local caching of variables.

practiceQuestions.q: Difference between volatile and synchronized in Java?
practiceQuestions.a: volatile guarantees variable visibility across CPU caches without locks. synchronized provides both visibility and atomicity (mutual exclusion) for entire code blocks.

roadmaps.title: Python
roadmaps.description: Pythonic idioms, Generators, Decorators, GIL, Memory Management, and OOPs in Python.

topics.title: Decorators, Generators & Context Managers
topics.explanation: Decorators dynamically wrap functions to alter behavior. Generators produce lazy sequences with yield, conserving memory.
topics.codeExample:
def timer_decorator(func):
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        import time
        start = time.time()
        res = func(*args, **kwargs)
        print(f"Elapsed: {time.time() - start:.4f}s")
        return res
    return wrapper

practiceQuestions.q: What is Python GIL (Global Interpreter Lock)?
practiceQuestions.a: A mutex that protects Python objects, preventing multiple native threads from executing Python bytecodes simultaneously in CPython.

topics.title: Python Memory Model & OOPs
topics.explanation: Python manages memory via reference counting supplemented by a cyclic generational garbage collector.

practiceQuestions.q: How does Method Resolution Order (MRO) work in Python?
practiceQuestions.a: Python uses the C3 Linearization algorithm to determine the order in which base classes are searched when calling a method on an instance.

roadmaps.title: DSA
roadmaps.description: Arrays, Strings, Linked Lists, Trees, Graphs, Dynamic Programming, Greedy, and Sorting.

topics.title: Arrays, Two Pointers & Sliding Window
topics.explanation: Arrays offer contiguous memory and O(1) index access. Sliding window reduces O(N^2) subarray problems to linear O(N).

practiceQuestions.q: How does Kadane's algorithm find maximum subarray sum in O(N)?
practiceQuestions.a: Maintains current_sum = max(x, current_sum + x) and max_sum = max(max_sum, current_sum).

topics.title: Binary Trees, BST, DFS, BFS & Shortest Paths
topics.explanation: Trees are hierarchical acyclic graphs. Graph traversals (DFS/BFS) form the backbone of pathfinding, cycle detection, and connectivity.

practiceQuestions.q: When should you use Bellman-Ford over Dijkstra?
practiceQuestions.a: Dijkstra fails on graphs with negative edge weights. Bellman-Ford handles negative weights and detects negative weight cycles in O(V * E).

topics.title: Dynamic Programming & Memoization
topics.explanation: Dynamic Programming solves problems with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure by caching subproblem solutions.

practiceQuestions.q: How to optimize LIS from O(N^2) to O(N log N)?
practiceQuestions.a: Using patience sorting with binary search (std::lower_bound or bisect) maintaining a tails array of smallest tail values for increasing subsequences.

roadmaps.title: DBMS
roadmaps.description: Relational model, ACID properties, Normalization, Indexing (B-Tree/B+ Tree), Transactions, and Concurrency Control.

topics.title: ACID Properties, Normalization (1NF to BCNF)
topics.explanation: ACID ensures reliable database transaction processing even during power failures or concurrent updates.

practiceQuestions.q: What are the 4 Transaction Isolation Levels and anomalies they prevent?
practiceQuestions.a: Read Uncommitted (allows dirty reads), Read Committed (prevents dirty reads), Repeatable Read (prevents non-repeatable reads), Serializable (prevents phantom reads).

topics.title: B+ Tree Indexing & Concurrency Protocols
subtopics: Why B+ Trees over B Trees in databases
topics.explanation: B+ Trees keep all data records in leaf nodes connected by a linked list, making range queries exceptionally fast with minimal disk I/O.
topics.codeExample: CREATE INDEX idx_user_status_date ON users(status, created_at);

practiceQuestions.q: Why do databases prefer B+ Trees over Binary Search Trees or Hash tables for indexing?
practiceQuestions.a: B+ Trees have high fan-out (low depth, minimizing disk seek time) and linked leaf nodes for O(range) sequential scanning, which hash tables cannot do.

roadmaps.title: Operating Systems
roadmaps.description: Process management, Threads, CPU scheduling, Virtual Memory, Paging, Deadlocks, and File Systems.

topics.title: Processes, Threads & Synchronization
topics.explanation: A process is a program in execution with its own address space; threads share address space and code while having private registers and stack.

practiceQuestions.q: What is the critical section problem and how does Peterson's solution work?
practiceQuestions.a: A region where concurrent processes access shared resources. Peterson's solution uses two flags and a turn variable to satisfy mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting for 2 processes.

topics.title: Virtual Memory, Paging & Page Replacement
topics.explanation: Virtual memory separates user logical memory from physical memory, permitting huge programs to run on limited RAM using demand paging.
topics.codeExample: Physical Address = (Frame Number * Page Size) + Offset

practiceQuestions.q: What causes Thrashing in an operating system and how to resolve it?
practiceQuestions.a: Thrashing occurs when the system spends more time servicing page faults than executing instructions. Solved by increasing RAM or using Working Set Model / Page Fault Frequency control.

roadmaps.title: Computer Networks
roadmaps.description: OSI vs TCP/IP model, TCP 3-way handshake, UDP, DNS, HTTP/HTTPS, Subnetting, Routing protocols.

topics.title: Transport Layer: TCP vs UDP & Handshake
topics.explanation: TCP guarantees reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery of packets via acknowledgments and sequence numbers. UDP offers low-latency connectionless datagram streaming.
topics.codeExample:
Client               Server
  | --- SYN (seq=x) --> |
  | <-- SYN-ACK (x+1, y)-|
  | --- ACK (seq=y+1) ->|
Connection Established!

practiceQuestions.q: What happens when you enter a URL in your browser address bar?
practiceQuestions.a: 1. DNS resolution (browser cache -> OS -> resolver -> root -> TLD -> authoritative). 2. TCP handshake (port 443/80). 3. TLS negotiation for HTTPS. 4. HTTP GET request sent. 5. Server responds. 6. Browser renders HTML/CSS/JS.

topics.title: Network Layer, Subnetting & TLS/HTTPS
subtopics: IPv4 vs IPv6 addressing & CIDR notation
topics.explanation: Network security hinges on asymmetric key exchange (RSA/Diffie-Hellman) negotiating a session key for blazing-fast symmetric encryption (AES).
topics.codeExample:
Subnet: 192.168.1.0/24
Netmask: 255.255.255.0
Total Hosts: 2^(32-24) - 2 = 254 usable IPs

practiceQuestions.q: Explain how SSL/TLS Handshake establishes a secure HTTPS session.
practiceQuestions.a: Client sends ClientHello (supported ciphers). Server responds with ServerHello and Digital Certificate. Client verifies certificate with CA, encrypts pre-master secret using server public key. Both derive symmetric session keys.

roadmaps.title: OOPs
roadmaps.description: Object-Oriented Programming principles: Encapsulation, Abstraction, Inheritance, Polymorphism, SOLID principles, and Design Patterns.

topics.title: The 4 Pillars of OOPs
topics.explanation: The 4 pillars form the foundation of modular, reusable, extensible, and maintainable software architecture in enterprise engineering.

practiceQuestions.q: What is the key difference between Abstraction and Encapsulation?
practiceQuestions.a: Abstraction focuses on hiding background implementation details and exposing only essential behavior (outer view). Encapsulation binds data and methods together and protects internal state via access modifiers (inner view).

practiceQuestions.q: Why does Java not support multiple inheritance with classes?
practiceQuestions.a: To avoid the Diamond Problem (ambiguity when two parent classes implement the same method). Java supports multiple inheritance through interfaces.

topics.title: SOLID Principles & Design Patterns
topics.explanation: SOLID principles guide developers to design clean, decoupled systems that are easy to test, maintain, and extend without breaking existing behavior.

practiceQuestions.q: Explain Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) with a classic violation example.
practiceQuestions.a: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering program correctness. Classic violation: Square inheriting from Rectangle where setting width modifies height.

roadmaps.title: SQL
roadmaps.description: Advanced SQL queries, Multi-table Joins, Aggregations, Window Functions, Subqueries, CTEs, and Stored Procedures.

topics.title: Multi-Table Joins & Grouped Aggregations
subtopics: INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER, CROSS, SELF JOIN
Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX)
topics.explanation: SQL joins connect related records across relational tables based on common keys, while GROUP BY collapses rows into summary metrics.
topics.codeExample:
SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS total_employees, AVG(e.salary) AS avg_salary
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name
HAVING COUNT(e.emp_id) >= 3
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;

practiceQuestions.q: What is the execution order of an SQL query?
practiceQuestions.a: FROM & JOIN -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT / OFFSET.

topics.title: Window Functions & Common Table Expressions (CTEs)
subtopics: PARTITION BY & ORDER BY in OVER clause
LEAD() and LAG() for running comparisons
topics.explanation: Window functions perform calculations across a set of table rows related to the current row without collapsing the rows into a single group.

practiceQuestions.q: How to find the N-th highest salary in SQL without window functions vs with window functions?
practiceQuestions.a: With window: SELECT salary FROM (SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER(ORDER BY salary DESC) as rk FROM employees) t WHERE rk = N; Without: SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees e1 WHERE N-1 = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.salary > e1.salary);

roadmaps.title: Aptitude
roadmaps.description: Quantitative aptitude, arithmetic formulas, rapid mental math, speed, time, work, and probability for placement tests.

topics.title: Percentages, Profit & Loss, Simple & Compound Interest
subtopics: Cost Price, Selling Price, Marked Price, Discount
Compound Interest vs Simple Interest difference formula
topics.explanation: Arithmetic aptitude tests problem-solving speed and accuracy under strict countdown clocks in campus placement rounds.
topics.codeExample:
Net change for successive changes of a% and b% = (a + b + (a*b)/100)%
CI - SI for 2 years = P * (R/100)^2

practiceQuestions.q: If price of a commodity increases by 25%, by what percent must consumption be reduced to keep expenditure constant?

topics.title: Time & Work, Pipes & Relative Speed
subtopics: Efficiency ratios and alternate day work
Pipes and cisterns with inlet/outlet rates
Relative speed for trains crossing poles and each other
topics.explanation: Work and speed problems can be solved in seconds using LCM as total work and calculating individual unit efficiencies per hour/day.
topics.codeExample:
Total Work = LCM(days taken by individuals)
Efficiency = Total Work / Time
Combined Time = Total Work / (Eff_A + Eff_B)

practiceQuestions.q: A can do a piece of work in 10 days, B in 15 days. They work together for 3 days, then A leaves. How long will B take to finish remaining work?
practiceQuestions.a: LCM(10, 15) = 30 units. A rate = 3 u/day, B rate = 2 u/day. 3 days combined = 3 * 5 = 15 units done. Remaining = 15 units. B takes 15 / 2 = 7.5 days.

roadmaps.title: Logical Reasoning
roadmaps.description: Syllogisms, Blood Relations, Seating Arrangements, Coding-Decoding, Direction Sense, and Critical Thinking.

topics.title: Syllogisms & Deductive Logic
subtopics: All, Some, No, Some Not rules
topics.explanation: Syllogisms test formal deductive logic by deriving valid conclusions from given premise statements regardless of real-world facts.
topics.codeExample:
Premise 1: All A are B.
Premise 2: Some B are C.
Conclusion: Some A are C -> (Does NOT strictly follow, only a possibility).

practiceQuestions.q: Statements: All pens are books. All books are markers. Conclusions: I. All pens are markers. II. Some markers are pens.
practiceQuestions.a: Both conclusions I and II follow. Since Pen subset of Book subset of Marker, all pens are markers and some markers are pens.

topics.title: Blood Relations & Seating Arrangements
subtopics: Family tree conventions (+ for male, - for female, = for couple)
Coded blood relations (A + B means A is father)
topics.explanation: Seating arrangements test constraint satisfaction and multi-variable deduction, common in Capgemini, TCS, and Infosys exams.
topics.codeExample:
Generation 1: Grandparents
Generation 2: Parents, Uncles, Aunts
Generation 3: Self, Siblings, Cousins

practiceQuestions.q: Pointing to a photograph, a man says, "She is the daughter of my grandfather's only son." Who is she to the man?
practiceQuestions.a: Grandfather's only son is the man's father. The daughter of the father is the man's Sister.

roadmaps.title: Verbal Ability
roadmaps.description: Reading comprehension, Sentence correction, Error spotting, Para jumbles, Synonyms, Antonyms, and Business Communication.

topics.title: Sentence Correction & Spotting Errors
topics.explanation: Sentence correction assesses grammatical rigor, syntax precision, and idiomatic correctness essential for corporate communication.
topics.codeExample:
Incorrect: "Neither the manager nor the employees was present."
Correct: "Neither the manager nor the employees WERE present." (Verb agrees with the closer subject).

practiceQuestions.q: Spot error: "One of the students who has completed the project was awarded the scholarship."
practiceQuestions.a: Error is "who has completed". In relative clauses modifying a plural noun ("students"), the verb should be plural: "who HAVE completed".

topics.title: Reading Comprehension & Para Jumbles
subtopics: Main idea vs supporting detail identification
topics.explanation: Reading comprehension evaluates speed reading and context inference, while para jumbles test logical flow and discourse cohesion.
topics.codeExample:
Para Jumble Strategy:
1. Find independent opening sentence (no pronouns like "they", "he", "this").
2. Locate noun-pronoun mandatory pairs.
3. Identify concluding sentence.

practiceQuestions.q: How to quickly identify the introductory sentence of a Para Jumble?
practiceQuestions.a: Look for a broad sentence introducing the central theme or proper nouns, devoid of dangling contrast words (However, Although) or pronouns referring back to unintroduced antecedents.

codingQuestions.title: Two Sum
codingQuestions.description:
Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target.

You may assume that each input would have exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice.

You can return the answer in any order.

codingQuestions.title: Reverse Linked List
codingQuestions.description: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list, and return the reversed list.
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is the range [0, 5000].

templates.python:
def reverseList(head):
    prev = None
    curr = head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt
    return prev

codingQuestions.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
codingQuestions.description:
You are given the heads of two sorted linked lists list1 and list2.

Merge the two lists into one sorted list. The list should be made by splicing together the nodes of the first two lists.

Return the head of the merged linked list.
constraints: The number of nodes in both lists is in the range [0, 50].

codingQuestions.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
codingQuestions.description: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without duplicate characters.

examples.explanation: The answer is "abc", with the length of 3.

constraints: s consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces.

codingQuestions.title: Trapping Rain Water
codingQuestions.description: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining.

codingQuestions.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
codingQuestions.description:
You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the ith day.

You want to maximize your profit by choosing a single day to buy one stock and choosing a different day in the future to sell that stock.

Return the maximum profit you can achieve from this transaction. If you cannot achieve any profit, return 0.

examples.explanation: Buy on day 2 (price = 1) and sell on day 5 (price = 6), profit = 6-1 = 5.

codingQuestions.title: Valid Parentheses
codingQuestions.description:
Given a string s containing just the characters "(", ")", "{", "}", "[" and "]", determine if the input string is valid.

An input string is valid if open brackets are closed by the same type of brackets and in the correct order.

codingQuestions.title: Maximum Subarray (Kadane)
codingQuestions.description: Given an integer array nums, find the subarray with the largest sum, and return its sum.

examples.explanation: The subarray [4,-1,2,1] has the largest sum 6.

codingQuestions.title: Container With Most Water
codingQuestions.description:
You are given an integer array height of length n. There are n vertical lines drawn such that the two endpoints of the ith line are (i, 0) and (i, height[i]).

Find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container, such that the container contains the most water.

Return the maximum amount of water a container can store.

codingQuestions.title: 3Sum
codingQuestions.description:
Given an integer array nums, return all the triplets [nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]] such that i != j, i != k, and j != k, and nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0.

Notice that the solution set must not contain duplicate triplets.

technicalQuestions.a: 3NF requires that every non-prime attribute is non-transitively dependent on candidate keys. BCNF is stricter: for every functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a super key.

A process is an execution unit with dedicated virtual memory. A thread is a lightweight flow within a process sharing heap, code, and global variables.

aptitudeQuestions.q: If 12 men can complete a work in 16 days, how many men are required to finish it in 24 days?

questionBank.question: What is the difference between a Binary Search Tree (BST) and an AVL Tree? Why is AVL self-balancing?
questionBank.answer:
A BST satisfies the invariant that left subtree keys < node key < right subtree keys. However, standard BST can degenerate into a linked list with O(N) worst-case time complexity upon skewed insertions.

An AVL tree is a strictly self-balancing BST where the difference in heights of left and right subtrees (Balance Factor = height(left) - height(right)) for any node cannot exceed {-1, 0, 1}. If insertion/deletion violates this balance, it executes O(1) single (LL, RR) or double (LR, RL) rotations, guaranteeing O(log N) lookup, insertion, and deletion.

questionBank.question: Explain Two-Phase Locking (2PL) protocol and how it ensures serializability.
questionBank.answer:
2PL is a concurrency control method that guarantees serializability through two distinct phases:
1. Growing Phase: A transaction can acquire locks (Shared or Exclusive) but cannot release any lock.
2. Shrinking Phase: Once a transaction releases its first lock, it cannot acquire any new lock; it can only release remaining locks.

The point where the transaction acquires its final lock is called the Lock Point. By ordering transactions by their lock points, 2PL prevents conflicts and ensures conflict serializability.

questionBank.question: What are SOLID principles in Object-Oriented Design?
questionBank.answer:
SOLID stands for:
1. Single Responsibility Principle (SRP): A class should have only one reason to change.
2. Open/Closed Principle (OCP): Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification.
3. Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP): Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without breaking client code.
4. Interface Segregation Principle (ISP): Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use.
5. Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP): High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions.

questionBank.question: What is a Race Condition and how do Semaphores and Mutexes prevent it?
questionBank.answer:
A Race Condition occurs in concurrent execution when the final outcome of multiple threads depends on the non-deterministic order of execution or timing. It happens when multiple threads access shared mutable data without proper synchronization.

- Mutex (Mutual Exclusion): A locking mechanism owned by a single thread. Only the thread that acquired the lock can release it.
- Semaphore: A signaling mechanism with an integer counter. Wait/P() decrements counter, Signal/V() increments counter. Counting semaphores allow access to N concurrent resources.
